data.title: Proving You're Human: From Dead Souls to the Iris and Palm Print Identity Business
data.description:
Author: Thejaswini M A, The Token Dispatch; Translator: Deep Tide TechFlow

In his satirical novel *Dead Souls*, published in 1842, Gogol told the story of acquiring lists of deceased serfs to serve as paper assets. In today's internet, with artificial intelligence capable of cheaply and mass-producing fake virtual identities, similar problems have resurfaced. The question of how much it is worth to prove the existence of a real human behind a screen is shifting from a theoretical problem to a mechanism with market pricing. This article outlines the technical paths and economic logic of CAPTCHAs, black market SMS verification codes, proof-of-work, and Worldcoin iris and vein/palmprint recognition.

The Dead Souls Problem in the Digital World

A well-dressed stranger arrives in a small provincial town in Russia and begins to pay for the names of serfs who have died but have not yet been removed from the official census list.

This is the plot of Gogol's 1842 novel *Dead Souls*. This practice made sense at the time because Russian landowners were required to pay taxes based on the number of serfs under their names, and the census was only updated every few years.

Landlords want to evade the taxes levied on the deceased, while buyers can apply for mortgage loans from the national bank by holding a nominal person on paper. The logic of history is clear: any system that provides benefits based on the number of people but cannot verify the authenticity of the entity will eventually be rife with fake accounts. In the early decades of the internet, becoming one person online was completely free; impersonating multiple people was also free. Websites allowed multiple email addresses to be registered, social media platforms allowed the use of aliases, and the blockchain world allowed one person to generate tens of thousands of wallet addresses in an afternoon. Once the system gives each account a vote, or issues an equivalent airdrop to each wallet, those who can create accounts at the lowest cost will get the largest share. Therefore, proof of human identity is not only an identity authentication technology, but also an economic technology. Since the internet needs to prove human identity, the key question is: what is the price of this proof? The Economic Costs of Black Market SMS Verification Codes A research team at Cambridge University has been tracking the cost of purchasing SMS verification codes, one of the most common anti-counterfeiting authentication measures. These prices fluctuate constantly with market demand. For example, on December 19, 2025, the cost of obtaining a Telegram verification code was $0.34, Facebook $0.21, and WhatsApp $0.25. The mass production of fake accounts has itself formed an independent supply and demand market.

Image: SMS verification codes and black market prices for fake accounts

A common method for creating fake accounts is using SIM cards. In September 2025, the U.S. Secret Service seized 300 SIM centralization servers and 100,000 prepaid SIM cards. The criminal gang used this hardware to register tens of thousands of social media and payment accounts in bulk.

A common method for creating fake accounts is using SIM cards.

Image: Source cotsi

Another cost is the time invested by society as a whole. According to relevant research estimates, global internet users spend approximately 500 person-years of their time each day on CAPTCHA verification codes such as identifying distorted letters and choosing traffic lights. If calculated based on the US minimum wage, the value of the time lost in recognizing CAPTCHAs annually is approximately $1.3 billion.

Even so, automated scripts and robots are learning to crack these tests.

In 2024, research teams had already achieved a 100% machine cracking rate for mainstream graphical CAPTCHAs using multimodal visual models. The idea behind encrypted networks: no longer counting users. The crypto industry calls this type of fake account attack a Sybil attack, a name derived from a classic paper published in 2002 by Microsoft researcher John Douceur. Satoshi Nakamoto's design for Bitcoin was to simply stop counting users. Nakamoto knew that voting by IP address wouldn't work because one person could easily rent a large number of proxy IPs. Bitcoin binds voting power to computing power; miners prove their participation by consuming electricity to calculate hash values, i.e., Proof-of-Work (PoW). The later Proof-of-Stake (PoS) further bound governance rights to staked capital. Both computing power and capital are truly scarce resources and cannot be infinitely replicated by simply registering accounts out of thin air. However, in scenarios where benefits need to be distributed based on real individuals, a system purely based on capital weighting still cannot solve the need for one person, one vote. Worldcoin's Orb Iris Solution and Dedicated Hardware Bottlenecks Worldcoin (formerly Worldcoin) attempts to return to the path of direct human identification, using the customized hardware device Orb. Orb collects the user's face and iris using an infrared camera to confirm that the individual is a real human and has not been registered twice, then generates a unique digital identity credential. Official data shows that more than 18 million people have completed the verification. Worldcoin's technological logic lies in the fact that dedicated biometric hardware can provide extremely high human uniqueness and anti-counterfeiting capabilities. If a regular mobile phone camera can capture irises, hackers could use fake cameras to inject forged digital video streams. To prevent this, World must manufacture its own Orb hardware and strictly control the sensors, lenses, and lighting environment. However, dedicated hardware also presents structural challenges in deployment: the higher the precision of the device, the higher the barriers to production, transportation, and coverage. For data storage, World employs a Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) scheme, dividing users' iris codes into encrypted fragments and distributing them across servers in different institutions, preventing a single centralized institution from controlling the entire biometric database. However, in terms of security, decentralized biometrics still faces the challenge of calculating the cost of attacks. Attacking Bitcoin requires purchasing huge amounts of electricity, attacking a PoS chain requires buying expensive tokens, and in a biometric system, if the value of airdropped tokens in a poor area exceeds the daily cost of living for local residents, hackers can often organize intermediaries to lure real residents offline with small amounts of cash for eye scanning, and then resell the tokens for arbitrage. The technological evolution of palmprint and vein recognition: Besides iris recognition, palm-based biometric solutions are also accelerating their commercialization. Amazon launched Amazon One palmprint payment for physical retail checkout, and Tencent's WeChat launched WeChat palm scanning, which has been deployed in rail transit gates and convenience stores. Palm recognition mainly combines two features: the palm print texture of the epidermis, and the subcutaneous vein distribution structure under near-infrared light. Because subcutaneous veins possess specific infrared absorption characteristics only when blood is flowing in living tissue, they are significantly more difficult to forge than ordinary flat facial photographs. From a user experience perspective, extending a palm provides greater psychological comfort and public health acceptance than placing the eyes close to the metal ball. Users do not need to remove their sunglasses or bend over to face the camera, making it more in line with everyday habits when passing through turnstiles or cash registers.

Image: Case study of social network discussions on the security of palmprint authentication

However, its core trade-off is similar to World: to achieve an extremely high level of anti-counterfeiting security, it also requires the use of dedicated infrared vein sensors, and cannot rely solely on the widespread adoption of inexpensive ordinary mobile phone front-facing cameras.

Conclusion

From the paper serfs in Dead Souls to today's SMS black market and automated robots, as long as the system has a mechanism for distributing profits based on the number of people, the industry of creating fake accounts will always exist.

In an era of rampant synthetic content and intelligent agents, the boundary for recognizing real humans is gradually retreating from software code to biological entities. Whether it's iris scanning or palm prints, how to balance the security barriers of dedicated hardware with the convenience of global adoption will remain a core issue that the next stage of decentralized identity systems must answer.

data.title: Bitdeer maintains zero Bitcoin holdings; BitMine increased its holdings by 8,573 ETH last week.
data.description:
Golden Weekly is a weekly blockchain industry summary column launched by Golden Finance, covering key news, market and contract data, mining information, project updates, technological advancements, and other industry dynamics.

Bitcoin

Bitdeer maintains zero Bitcoin holdings, sold 258.6 BTC this week

On November 7th, Bitdeer released its weekly Bitcoin update on the X platform, stating that as of November 6th, its Bitcoin production this week was 258.6 BTC, all of which have been sold, resulting in a net increase of 0 BTC. Currently, its Bitcoin holdings are 0 (excluding customer deposits).

BlackRock Deposits 1883 BTC, Worth $143 Million, into Coinbase Prime On November 6th, BlackRock, through its subsidiary IBIT, deposited 1883 BTC, worth approximately $143 million, into Coinbase Prime. Elliptic: Approximately $50 Million in XRP Primarily Converted to Bitcoin On November 6th, according to The Defiant, citing on-chain analytics firm Elliptic, addresses related to the Binance hack have converted approximately $50 million in XRP into Bitcoin, primarily through THORChain. Approximately $226 million in XRP remains untransferred. Bitcoin obtained from other stolen assets nearly doubled to 1650 within a day, while the majority of ETH and BTC holdings remain untransferred.

A whale that had been dormant for over a year bought 3009 BTC

On November 6th, according to Lookonchain monitoring, Bitcoin address 3Ps78…hm9F resumed activity after being dormant for over a year, buying a total of 3009 BTC that day, worth approximately $228 million.

Strive's Q3 net profit was $509 million, and it increased its BTC holdings

On November 6th, according to Strive's (ASST) Q3 2026 report, the company's revenue for the quarter was $2.696 million, net profit was approximately $509 million, net profit attributable to common shareholders was approximately $475 million, diluted earnings per share were $5.24, and unrealized net gains from digital assets were approximately $534 million.

In the third quarter, the company increased its holdings by 8,136 BTC, at an average cost of $78,885 per BTC; as of September 30, it held 28,000 BTC with a fair value of approximately $2.34 billion, and cash and cash equivalents of approximately $285 million. From October 1 to 30, it purchased another 15,124 BTC at an average price of approximately $83,310 (including fees and expenses); as of October 30, its total Bitcoin holdings increased to 43,124 BTC, and cash and cash equivalents of approximately $490 million. Ethereum (ETH)

glassnode: US Spot Ethereum ETF Sees 23 Consecutive Trading Days of Net Outflows, Setting a New Record for the Longest Consecutive Net Outflows Since Listing

On November 1st, Glassnode published an article on its X platform stating that ETF investors are withdrawing from ETH, with the US Spot Ethereum ETF experiencing 23 consecutive trading days of net outflows, setting a new record for the longest consecutive outflows since the product's listing. This reflects weak demand from traditional investors—who had made significant purchases in August and September.

Glassnode: US Spot Ethereum ETF Sees 23 Consecutive Trading Days of Net Outflows, Setting a New Record for the Longest Consecutive Outflows Since Listing

On November 5th, according to Lookonchain monitoring, the CryptoBilis Ledger attacker's address deposited approximately 885 ETH into Tornado Cash, worth approximately $2.14 million. On November 5th, Vitalik Buterin stated in an interview that in the coming years, Ethereum will utilize cutting-edge technologies, including GPUs, to achieve multi-tasking parallel processing while maintaining decentralization. The Ethereum Foundation will focus on its areas of expertise, providing support to developers in terms of technical capabilities, security, privacy, and openness; areas outside its expertise will be left to users and the community to explore. BitMine increased its holdings by 8,573 ETH last week, bringing its total holdings to approximately 6.06 million ETH. As of November 1, 2026, its total ETH holdings reached 6,060,506 ETH, representing approximately 4.9% of the total ETH supply. Currently, BitMine holds approximately $14.5 billion in cryptocurrency, cash, and other investment assets, including $498 million in cash and securities, 216 Bitcoins, $180 million in equity assets in Beast Industries, and an $82 million investment in Eightco Holdings (ORBS). Furthermore, it has staked 5,227,037 ETH (86% of its total holdings), valued at approximately $11.8 billion at $2,261 per ETH, with a current annualized staking yield of approximately $358 million. Ethereum Core Developers Meeting Postpones Hoodi Testnet Fork On November 6th, the Ethereum Foundation announced that security firm ChainSecurity recently discovered that certain invariants relied upon by some projects may become invalid after the Glamsterdam upgrade. This involves adjustments to some operation gas fees and state gas billing methods in EIP-8037 and EIP-8038. The Ethereum Core Developers Meeting (ACD) decided to postpone the hard fork process and will not launch a fork on the Hoodi testnet until the issue is resolved. The Foundation stated that it is currently working with several auditing firms to review and conduct internal audits, but this cannot cover all on-chain and off-chain code of all projects. It urged contract developers and auditors to self-check whether they rely on the relevant eight invariants and has created a dedicated GitHub repository providing invariant explanations, examples, and self-check tips. Other Projects

Uniswap Confirms Support for V4 Hooks on Hyperliquid L2 Project Elysium

On November 7th, according to HL HUB (Community), Uniswap confirmed support for V4 Hooks on the Hyperliquid L2 project Elysium. Developers can use Uniswap V4 Hooks to build customizable liquidity pools with features such as dynamic fees and custom trading logic. The Elysium mainnet is expected to officially launch on November 9th.

... OpenAI CFO: Data Center Investments Will Not Change Due to Midterm Election On November 7th, OpenAI CFO Sarah Freer stated in an interview with CNBC that the company will not change its AI infrastructure investment plans due to the US midterm election results. It will continue to collaborate with major hyperscale cloud service providers and meet AI customer needs through financing. She believes the election results will not significantly change the company's business, but with increased attention on data centers, OpenAI will continue to strengthen communication and build trust with local communities. In this midterm election, of the 41 local data center-related votes in 10 states, only one did not support measures to restrict construction or opposed measures to support development. Voters were primarily concerned about data centers driving up electricity costs, damaging the environment, and impacting jobs. Freer stated that OpenAI secretly filed for an IPO with the SEC in June and is considering a 2027 listing, while also negotiating a new round of financing at a pre-money valuation of $1.25 trillion. She emphasized that the demand for AI is real and continues to grow.

Coinbase Launches USDC Borrowing with PAXG Collateral

On November 6th, Coinbase announced on its X platform that users can now instantly borrow USDC using tokenized gold PAX Gold (PAXG) as collateral, gaining liquidity without selling assets. This feature is powered by Morpho, built on Base, and is currently available to users in the US (excluding New York State) and Canada.

Amazon Strengthens AI Shopping Strategy, Launches Text-Based Shopping Feature with Alexa

On November 6th, Amazon launched a text-based shopping feature via Alexa. Amazon stated that this new text-based interaction feature helps users search and compare products, track promotions and price changes, and allows "Alexa for Shopping" to complete purchases on behalf of the user.

... Amazon says the feature is currently rolling out to a limited number of invited US users and is expected to expand its rollout in the coming weeks. This release comes after Amazon recently blocked Meta's AI shopping agent, Muse, from accessing its e-commerce platform. In addition, Amazon won a court ruling in March to prohibit Perplexity's shopping agent, Comet, from accessing its platform. However, a US appeals court overturned this injunction in August, and the related litigation is still ongoing.

Robot training simulation platform Physicl raises $10 million in seed funding

On November 6th, according to TechCrunch, robot training simulation platform Physicl raised $10 million in seed funding from Inovia Capital. The platform aims to help world model developers and robot manufacturers solve training problems through more realistic simulation environments. Physicl is launching its Studio product, offering 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 object assets for users to create scenes and generate synthetic training data; world model developer SpAItial is one of its early clients.

data.title: Dan Bin: The probability of the AI ​​era coming to an end is extremely small; funds will be recouped for further investment.
data.description:
Author: The Paper

US tech stocks experienced dramatic volatility this week. Under the dual pressures of questioned sustainability of AI infrastructure investment and stronger-than-expected non-farm payroll data boosting interest rate hike expectations, US tech stocks suffered an "epic" plunge on Thursday, only to rebound on Friday, driven by oversold chip stocks.

In response to market concerns about the prospects of AI investment, Dan Bin, Chairman of Oriental Harbor, stated on social media earlier on November 6th that Thursday's stock market crash was "a temporary shock, but the probability of judging the AI ​​era as over is extremely small."

Dan Bin has consistently been optimistic about artificial intelligence in recent years, with overseas markets being a major area of ​​investment.

Dan Bin believes that the market may be anticipating the impact of the draft "Artificial Superintelligence Ban Act" in the US, but the probability of the bill actually being implemented is low.

Dan Bin believes that the market may be reflecting the impact of the draft "Artificial Superintelligence Ban Act" in advance, but the probability of the bill actually being implemented is low.

The draft policies are still uncertain before they are officially implemented, and the long-term trend of the AI ​​industry will not be easily changed as a result. However, short-term market sentiment is easily swayed by eye-catching news. Later on November 6th, Dan Bin posted again, stating that the sharp drop in US stocks triggered a double-high selling strategy by overseas funds, and the recovered funds will continue to be used to increase holdings, with SpaceX (SPCX.O) as the target. As of the close of trading on November 6th, SpaceX (SPCX.O) rose 8.62%, closing at $134.27. However, after hitting a new high for the year at $176.42 on October 7, the stock price saw a maximum pullback of over 31% by November 6, with a cumulative decline of 21.52% in the past month. Earlier this week, some of Oriental Harbor's products attracted market attention due to a significant drop in net asset value in October, with the unit net asset value of Hongyuan Phase 2 falling to 0.6282 yuan. In response, Dan Bin stated on November 4th that this was true, as the product was bound by contract to invest only in A-shares and Hong Kong stocks, and heavily invested in the AI ​​industry chain, resulting in a significant drawdown. "Of course, I still have a positive outlook on artificial intelligence, including A-share and Hong Kong-listed companies in the AI ​​product chain, but I truly didn't expect them to fall like this." On November 5th, he further stated that approximately 90% of Oriental Harbor's assets under management are invested globally, and addressed external doubts based on the company's previous performance. On October 22, a 13F filing disclosed by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) revealed that as of the end of the third quarter of 2026, Oriental Harbor's overseas funds held 13 stocks, with a total disclosed market value of approximately US$1.469 billion. From the perspective of holdings structure, Google-C is the largest holding, with a market value of approximately $395 million, accounting for 26.92%; Nvidia ranks second, with a market value of approximately $281 million, accounting for 19.16%; Intel is the third largest holding, with a market value of $211.38 million, accounting for 14.39%; Micron Technology and SanDisk are the fourth and fifth largest holdings, respectively, accounting for 10.94% and 9.33%. These five stocks account for more than 80% of the disclosed US stock holdings, indicating a high concentration of holdings. In the third quarter of this year, Oriental Harbor continued to increase its holdings in Google-C, Nvidia, Micron Technology, and SanDisk. Among them, the number of shares held in Google-C increased by 10.54%, and the number of shares held in Nvidia increased by 13.72%. At the same time, the fund newly bought Apple and SpaceX, and completely sold its holdings in Marvell Technology and Arm Holdings plc ADR. This is SpaceX's first purchase.

data.title: Why should the crypto industry be alarmed by the collapse of a traditional bank in Paraguay?
data.description:
Author: @hmalviya9; Translator: AIdidiaoJP, Foresight News

I. Why a Paraguayan Bank's Crash Should Wake Up the Crypto Industry

A Paraguayan bank claiming approximately three million users experienced a temporary inability for its customers to access their accounts. People waiting to pay rent, buy food, or collect pensions suddenly found themselves unable to withdraw their money.

Reuters reported that Ueno Bank, which manages approximately $850 million in public funds, is under investigation for allegedly over-lending to companies linked to its controlling shareholder. On November 3, 2026, the Central Bank of Paraguay announced a resolution to Ueno—its solvency ratio, after adjustments to its financial statements, fell below half of the minimum requirement. Regulators stated that this was an issue specific to this institution, not a widespread problem across the national banking system.

But for someone waiting to pay rent, buy food, or collect a pension, the comfort of "the system's overall robustness" won't unlock their account. Deposit protection is important, but so is how quickly people can actually use their own money. The Paraguay incident should serve as a wake-up call for the crypto industry. When people lose access to the fruits of their labor, our answer must be something truly usable: a path to getting help, making payments, and having more control as they rebuild their lives. But before claiming to have such an alternative, we must first understand: which promises have failed? Can our own system uphold them? II. Banks are not piggy banks, and the crisis isn't "all banks are finished." Banks lend to make money. But who gets the credit, what the terms are, and how strict the review is—the decisions are still made by people and institutions. Financial statements are important, collateral is important, and sometimes relationships are important too. The danger begins when relationships replace due diligence—insiders get the money, and everyone bears the consequences. Corporate loans have limits. The Basel Large Exposures Framework typically stipulates that exposure to a single counterparty or related group cannot exceed 25% of a bank's Tier 1 capital, depending on the scope and exemptions. So the issue isn't just whether the rules exist, but whether they are enforced, whether related borrowers are identified, and whether losses are disclosed before depositors discover them through a locked app. Banks themselves are more complex than simply "accepting deposits and issuing loans." Banks create deposits when they lend, subject to capital, liquidity, regulatory, and economic constraints. Your balance is a claim against the bank, not a stack of cash in a box with your name on it. The capital shortfall exposed by Ueno also needs clarification. A bank having too little capital to absorb losses is not the same as "running out of reserves." Distinguishing this is crucial to determining the specific problems of the institution and the appropriateness of the bailout plan. However, it's also important to be precise: no bank is immune to failure, but this doesn't mean all banks are failing, nor does it mean every country is becoming like Paraguay. A liquidity shortage means an institution cannot pay its debts on time; insolvency means its financial position cannot bear its obligations. Central banks can help resolve liquidity issues, but someone must ultimately bear the actual losses. III. Uneven Distribution of Global Financial Resilience: Don't Mistake the "Worst-Case" for the "Whole Picture" The global landscape contains both resilience and real damage. Banks insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) earned $90.1 billion in the second quarter of 2026, and the FDIC reported strong capital and liquidity. The claim of a "complete collapse of the global banking system" doesn't align with the data. Before Ueno's disposal, the IMF reported in May 2026 that Paraguay's total system capital adequacy ratio was 17.3%, above the minimum requirement of 12%. However, a healthy overall ratio does not prove that every bank is healthy. In September 2026, IMF staff were still urging Lebanon to restructure its banks and protect depositors through proper loss allocation. The banking crisis could escalate into a protracted tug-of-war: who will absorb the losses? The latest World Bank update shows that Sri Lanka's GDP has returned to pre-crisis levels, but the estimated poverty rate in 2025 is 16.9%, still higher than before the crisis. National output recovery does not equate to household recovery. Regarding external debt in developing economies, the World Bank reports $9.4 trillion in outstanding debt in 2025, with $1.4 trillion in principal and interest payments due that year. Debt repayment pressures will eat up resources that could be used for investment and public services. The World Bank also reports that the average interest rate on new bonds issued by the poorest eligible borrowers in 2025 will be 9.4%. Some governments are refinancing old debt at high interest rates. Borrowing can finance productive growth, but as repayments continue to crowd out investment, ordinary people experience fewer opportunities and weaker services. This isn't evidence of "the worst economy in our real history," but rather evidence of "uneven distribution of financial resilience." The IMF's October 2026 assessment stated that the global banking system is generally resilient, but also warned of weak banks, sovereign debt pressures, leverage, and liquidity risks in the non-bank sector. Both can be true simultaneously. Governments also have varying degrees of room for maneuver. Issuing your own currency gives you options, but it doesn't equate to unlimited purchasing power. Printing currency doesn't create foreign exchange, import fuel, food, or production capacity. The US enjoys the advantage of the dollar's international role, but it can't escape inflation, interest costs, and confidence issues. IV. After the collapse of trust, crypto must answer "What will it replace?" When institutions break their promises, people question not only the institutions themselves, but also the arrangements that made them dependent on them. A person's savings represent time, labor, and sacrifice. Losing access to these savings can turn financial failure into a legitimacy crisis. This won't automatically lead to widespread adoption of encryption. It may spur demand for stronger state protection, stricter regulations, or alternative systems. The outcome depends in part on which alternative actually works. Stablecoins can provide immediate relief. Given a weak local currency, there are reasons to prefer a digital dollar, especially for cross-border payments. But dollar tokens don't eliminate all dependencies; they may introduce dependence on the issuer, reserve custodian, redemption arrangements, and the dollar itself. Circle explicitly states its ability to block addresses from sending or receiving USDC. Holding a private key doesn't necessarily equate to unconditional control of the token. Self-custody and censorship resistance by the issuer are two different things. This raises a recurring question: Are we building another monetary economy, or are we expanding the distribution channels of the existing monetary economy? Both can produce useful products, but we must be honest about the differences. Stablecoins can improve accessibility while retaining centralized control. Privacy can hide a payment but doesn't eliminate the issuer's right to freeze funds. Putting things on the blockchain doesn't solve the question of who ultimately decides. Zcash is noteworthy because shielding transactions protects transaction information from public view. But wallets and transaction paths are crucial: Zcash also supports transparent transactions. Privacy doesn't make ZEC a stable store of purchasing power. People recovering from the banking crisis shouldn't be peddled with the idea that "buying volatility guarantees certainty." World ID solves a different problem: proving someone is a unique individual without requiring them to reveal their identity. This can help distribution programs reduce duplicate payments. But it doesn't create funds for a universal basic income, and obtaining an identity certificate doesn't equate to obtaining income rights. Here's a direction worth exploring: a basic income safety net plus earning opportunities. But the source of income must be genuine. Payments can be supported by fees, public revenue, cooperative profits, or a well-funded endowment fund. A rising token price is not a permanent social budget. Even a $100 million fund has its limits. Theoretically, $1 can cover 100 million people, not even considering costs. Giving $10 to 1 million people per month would cost $120 million a year. The first experiment tested distribution; the second requires a sustainable economic model. Fifth, "Human Commitment Markets": Separating Help from Earning, and Making Validation Proven. This is precisely the connection point I'm referring to as "Human Commitment Markets." Emergency support should help people, not require them to "earn" their right to survival. At the same time, the community can fund people to voluntarily commit: learning mobile phone repair, completing an apprenticeship, maintaining open-source tools, teaching a useful skill, or providing community service. Before work begins, clearly define the commitments, deadlines, compensation, and evidence. Payment should be held in escrow. The instructor's obligations should also be clearly stated. Learners should not lose money due to a missing instructor, biased assessors, or unfulfilled promised training. Those without savings should be able to participate through sponsored slots, not be barred from entry by mandatory deposits. The challenge lies in verification. Code can release funds after signature verification, but it cannot independently determine if someone has learned to repair a phone. Practical assessments, multiple assessors, appeals, and accountability-based dispute resolution remain crucial. Reputation should be built on fulfilled commitments, coupled with selective disclosure, rather than becoming a permanent public record of every failure. This is what I want to explore: the "sharing economy around tokens": people use marketplaces to coordinate useful work, accumulate skills, and share value. Tokens are only useful when they improve these relationships. Cryptocurrency does not eliminate human trust. It can reduce certain forms of discretion and make certain promises easier to verify. Smart contracts can still have bugs, follow manipulated oracles, or give administrators too much power. "Code guarantees you'll never be fooled" is marketing. The real question is: what promises does the code actually fulfill, and who can change them? Therefore, accelerate crypto-autonomy—understood as voluntary coordination, privacy, and freedom to opt out. Build alternative systems before people are forced to find alternatives in a crisis. Sixth, for technology to be implemented, privacy, identity, and recovery are all essential. Ethereum privacy requires work on multiple levels. Kohaku is a privacy-focused wallet implementation and SDK; its wallet repository is currently marked as under active development and only supports the Sepolia testnet. It is a foundational component, not a finished, mass-market emergency wallet. XMTP provides end-to-end encrypted messaging, and its security documentation acknowledges observable connection metadata. Nym handles network metadata through network mixing. These tools address different problems and require careful integration. Transaction privacy, communication privacy, and network access privacy are three distinct requirements. Good design also requires available recovery, reliable infrastructure, and clear limitations on administrator power. The strength of a privacy statement depends on how much information is exposed around it. The idea of ​​physical QR codes makes this understandable. A person scans a code, receives a small payment, and learns to transfer or spend it. Using ERC-5564, a QR code can encode a stealthy meta-address from which new receiving addresses can be derived. This reduces the public association with the recipient but does not hide the transaction amount, sender, or subsequent transactions that might re-associate the identity. Printed QR codes must never expose the spending key. Start with small, voluntary pilot programs, leveraging trusted local communities, including those supporting those affected by banking disruptions. Aid must never be contingent on participating in protests, supporting political stances, abandoning biometrics, or purchasing tokens. A useful example is: a person can receive help, control it, regain access, and spend it. A $1 transfer is a starting point, not proof of financial independence. The meaningful questions follow: Does this person use the wallet again? Can they pay local merchants? Are transaction fees eating up the payment? Can they recover it if their phone is lost? Does the app expose their social or financial relationships? Community funds can pay developer DAOs to address these issues through phased grants, independent security audits, and transparent spending accounts. Recipient identities can remain private, and organizations spending money should be held accountable. Donor influence should not quietly morph into permanent control of infrastructure. Identity, reputation, and privacy issues should also be handled in this way: prove uniqueness when projects require it, prove fulfilled promises when trust requires it, and disclose as little as possible beyond that. A company should not be the mandatory gatekeeper for these three aspects. We were building a trustless system, yet people in the crypto world find it difficult to trust each other. Rebuilding trust requires worthwhile commitments, and these commitments must be consistently fulfilled after launch: maintained software, accessible support, fair debate, transparent spending, and the ability to truly exit. If humans have created institutions for organizing life, we can create alternatives. The test is: when commitments break down, can these alternatives give ordinary people more control? A person should be able to access help, learn skills, earn income, communicate privately, and participate in communities, without surrendering their entire identity to an institution. That's a future worth building, and a more compelling reason for crypto's existence—far more meaningful than just another token code.

data.title: Is winning the bid the final straw? The market has already faced the potential pitfalls of AI "revolving financing."
data.description:
Author: Zhao Ying, Wall Street Insights

The cracks in the AI ​​boom narrative are widening. The day after the election, the Nasdaq suffered its biggest single-day drop since the COVID-19 pandemic, wiping out all year-to-date gains for technology funds. This turmoil has brought to the surface a structural vulnerability that the market had long deliberately ignored—AI-driven cyclical financing.

Ron Adler, co-head of global cash trading at JPMorgan Chase, stated bluntly in his latest market reflection that AI remains the core pillar of the current market. As hyperscale cloud computing companies begin to turn to the capital markets to raise funds for their ambitions, traders are taking advantage of this, pushing further down the risk curve, heavily buying upstream components and bottleneck assets.

However, the fragility of this chain of logic is now unavoidable.

"Revolving revenue has received a lot of attention, but the cyclical impact of AI on the market and the tech sector hasn't been adequately examined when the market is performing well," Adler said. "Now, all that has changed." This assessment is not accidental. On the same day, media outlets such as the Wall Street Journal extensively reported on the risks of AI-driven revolving financing, causing a sudden shift in market sentiment. The S&P 500 experienced its largest single-day drop since "Liberation Day," hedge funds faced significant pressure, and market trading volume surged by more than 50% compared to the previous trading day.

Circular Financing: An Overlooked Structural Risk

Adler's analysis reveals the core logic of AI transactions over the past few years: hyperscale cloud computing companies rely on their strong balance sheets to drive capital expenditures, which the market interprets as a continued strong industry fundamentals. This has spawned an investment chain extending outward from core computing power—"shovel and pickaxe" assets such as chips, optical communications, storage, and emerging cloud computing providers (neoclouds) have been successively bought, and risk appetite has continued to rise.

However, when these companies' expansion logic shifts from their own funds to financing from external capital markets, the circular problem emerges.

The so-called "circular financing" refers to the structure in the AI ​​industry chain where the revenue and financing needs of all parties are interdependent and mutually reinforcing. This positive cycle can reverse rapidly once capital market conditions tighten or market confidence wavers. Adler frankly admits that this risk has not received due attention during the market uptrend. Specific signals are quite clear: META is financing at a 7.5% interest rate, Marvell Technology (MRVL)'s stock price has cumulatively fallen by about 40% after announcing its deal with LITE, and hedge fund positions are under pressure. "The trades are already shaky," Adler writes, "and the election results may just be the last straw." Crowded trading pressure spreads to upstream and downstream sectors. Adler points out that crowded positions are the core pain point of the current market. Hedge fund long-short spread strategies were somewhat effective on the day, but after the activity of the previous trading day, long exposure still appears heavy. He stated that as the afternoon session drew to a close, inquiries from clients regarding pain points, factor risks, correlations, position sizing, and fund pressures continued to rise, indicating a high degree of correlation between market activity and anxiety. From a sector perspective, the impact has clearly spread to the entire AI industry chain: optical communication, memory chips, and emerging cloud computing providers have all suffered significant selling pressure. Adler observed that while the directional logic of the day's fund flows was reasonable, the magnitude of the sell-off surprised market participants. It is noteworthy that some of the selling was not due to a change in fundamental assessments, but rather appeared to be forced. "What we are seeing is partly portfolio-level pain and indiscriminate selling," he wrote. Meanwhile, many investors who had previously positioned themselves for a year-end rebound are now facing a shift in sentiment, with some choosing to exit the market, replacing their belief in holding with a sense of defeat. What is the risk of an economic recession? Internal Disagreements Emerge at JPMorgan Chase

Within the same report framework, Andrew Tyler, head of JPMorgan Chase's market intelligence team, and Adler's assessments show a clear divergence. Tyler's team maintains a tactical bullish stance, citing historical data that when the Nasdaq 100 index is within 6% of its historical high and experiences a single-day drop exceeding 3.5%, the index rebounds by an average of about 3% the following week, an effect particularly pronounced when the decline occurs on Friday. Tyler also addressed market concerns that a decline in AI capital expenditure could trigger an economic recession, giving a negative assessment. He cited several indicators: consumer household net worth is at historical highs, cash reserves are ample, and checking account balances are five times higher than before the COVID-19 pandemic; corporate profit margins are at or near historical highs, and large-scale layoffs are not yet a trigger; and the direct impact of AI on the job market is quite limited—for example, CoreWeave (CRWV), the epicenter of the storm, has only about 550 employees. Tyler concludes that the biggest impact of the AI ​​slowdown on the economy may be concentrated in the pressure on GDP growth caused by declining capital expenditures, rather than a comprehensive deterioration in the labor market or consumer spending; systemic risks at the economic level remain manageable at present.

data.title: Another blow – is Anthropic's IPO before the new year in jeopardy?
data.description:
Author: BitpushNews

Anthropic probably didn't expect that its carefully chosen listing window would be overturned by the midterm election.

On November 6th, Bloomberg reported that potential buyers were discussing lowering the valuation range to $1.2 trillion to $1.3 trillion, with some investors even considering the possibility of lowering it to $1.1 trillion. Just a month ago, the market was giving a figure of $2 trillion.

From $2 trillion to $1.1 trillion, three price cuts occurred in less than six weeks.

Data shows that the implied valuation of Anthropic's pre-IPO contracts on Hyperliquid has plummeted from $1.93 trillion to $1.58 trillion since the midterm election, a decrease of $340 billion, and the decline continued to widen during Friday's US trading session.

On Kalshi, the probability of Anthropic completing its IPO before November 30th dropped from 84% on Wednesday to 60% on Thursday; the probability of completing its IPO before December 31st dropped from 90% to 74%, and data from Polymarket showed similar results. From 95% to less than 60%, only a midterm election and a quarterly earnings report separated them. The $895 billion bill... If we only look at growth, Anthropic's Q3 is almost impeccable. Revenue reached $16.96 billion, a year-over-year increase of over 12 times, and a sequential increase of approximately 47% from Q2's $11.56 billion. The number of customers paying over $100,000 annually jumped from less than 1,000 a year ago to nearly 12,000. The net revenue retention rate is approximately 900%, indicating that existing customers are aggressively increasing their spending. However, risks lurk elsewhere. As of the end of September, Anthropic's total procurement commitments and lease agreements amounted to $895.4 billion, the vast majority of which is for computing power and infrastructure, with a timeframe extending to 2045. Of this, approximately $69.8 billion will mature within the next 12 months, and approximately $450 billion will mature before the end of 2030. Q3 spending on computing power and infrastructure reached $9.9 billion, more than 40% higher than Q2's $5.56 billion. The result is: while Q2 saw an operating profit of $974 million, Q3 turned into an operating loss of $567 million. Anthropic explained in its filing that some of its computing power was purchased from the short-term market because long-term contracts couldn't cover the surge in demand during the quarter, and short-term computing power was "currently much more expensive." This is precisely the reason for the $895 billion long-term commitment—replacing expensive spot supply with locked-in, cheaper forward supply. However, the market sees another side: a company with quarterly revenue of $17 billion signed a computing power bill equivalent to nearly seven times its cash reserves. As of the end of September, Anthropic had approximately $146.6 billion in cash, short-term investments, and available credit. $895 billion versus $146.6 billion—when AI capital expenditure is booming, it's called "seizing the opportunity"; when AI transactions begin to be questioned, it's called high leverage. The unfortunate timing: The November 3rd midterm elections saw the Democrats win both the House and Senate. Texas's newly elected Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, made a clear campaign promise to immediately halt data center development and has not retracted this statement after winning the election. Analysts at William Blair estimate that states supporting the data center halt order account for 40% of the nation's planned data center capacity. On Thursday, the Nasdaq 100 plummeted 5.8%, wiping out $2.1 trillion in market capitalization in a single day; the semiconductor ETF fell 10%, and all 11 sectors of the S&P 500 were affected. This was not a typical correction. Its trigger was a risk previously considered "unlikely" by the market: the physical expansion of AI infrastructure is beginning to encounter political resistance. Meta President Dina Powell McCormick publicly stated after the election that data center construction would become "more difficult." Anthropic's IPO roadshow was originally scheduled to begin the week of November 9th, with the listing date set for the week of November 16th. Four sources familiar with the matter interviewed by Reuters said potential investors are already doubting whether Anthropic can complete its roadshow on time; if pressure on AI assets persists, the company may postpone its move until the market is more stable. Wedbush Securities chip analyst Matt Bryson wrote in a report, "We believe Anthropic's October results and its successful IPO are important barometers of the health of the AI ​​market, as the former will be seen as an indicator of demand, while the latter is a key sign that AI-related companies can continue to raise funds to support their future growth plans." HSBC's chief multi-asset strategist Max Kettner said in a Bloomberg Radio interview that current AI deals are driven by a series of narratives, and he does not agree with the most popular narrative—that the AI ​​cycle is over. He believes that Anthropic's IPO is the biggest potential catalyst to reverse this situation, but only if the pricing is conservative enough, even below $1 trillion. Max Kettner also offered a contrasting scenario: the worst-case scenario is a repeat of SpaceX's IPO – opening enthusiasm quickly reversed, and the stock price hovered below the offering price for over a month. The conclusion is clear: Anthropic's IPO will either help the severely damaged AI sector regain its footing, or it will become yet another reason for investors to flee in droves.

data.title: US stock market crash and reversal: Is deleveraging nearing its end or the prelude to medium- to long-term risks?
data.description:
Author: Jae, PANews

In just two trading days, US stock market players experienced a rapid rollercoaster ride.

On November 5th, US stocks suffered their strongest single-day sell-off in nearly 19 months, with the AI ​​industry chain leading the decline. Rumors of "hedge funds collectively going bankrupt" quickly spread on social media, as if a financial storm was imminent.

Unexpectedly, the reversal came so quickly. On November 6th, chip stocks led the counterattack: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed up 4.2%, AMD surged 11%, and AI concept stocks such as Nvidia also rebounded; the Nasdaq closed up 1.1%, and the S&P 500 rose slightly by 0.3%.

This unexpected market movement may have been foreshadowed a month ago. Meanwhile, a cross-asset migration of funds is quietly unfolding. Deleveraging selling pressure has slowed, but medium- to long-term risks remain. The rebound on November 6th actually showed signs in the last ten minutes of trading on Thursday. Vanda Research data shows that US retail investors clearly shifted to buying near the close the previous day, with net purchases exceeding $100 million in the final 10 minutes. A more crucial variable comes from leveraged ETFs. According to Nomura Securities' calculations, to complete the net asset value rebalancing on November 5th, leveraged ETFs needed to sell approximately $47 billion in equity exposure before the close. This is the second-largest single-day sell-off since records began in 2006. When this massive wave of passive selling was completed before the close, the market's short-term selling pressure was significantly released. The combined forces of bargain-hunting funds, short covering, and institutional portfolio rebalancing jointly drove the price recovery. JPMorgan Chase pointed out in its post-market commentary that Thursday's aggressive deleveraging cleared some crowded trades, making the market's positioning structure healthier. In other words, last night's rebound was more of a short-term technical correction; the long-term contradictions such as shifting policy expectations and doubts about the returns on AI capital expenditure have not truly been resolved. The narrative of margin calls has been exaggerated; hedge funds deleveraged a month in advance. During this round of sharp fluctuations in US stocks, hedge funds became a focus of market attention. According to a Bloomberg report on November 5th, Tiger Global's flagship hedge fund lost approximately 8.5% in October, with its year-to-date returns roughly flat; Walleye Capital fell approximately 5.9% during the same period, with a year-to-date loss of approximately 6.8%; and Lone Pine Capital lost approximately 8.8% in a single month. Social media was subsequently flooded with panic narratives of "Wall Street hedge funds collectively going bankrupt." Walleye Capital, Engineers Gate, and Samlyn Capital, among others, announced team layoffs, strategy streamlining, and capital returns to investors, exacerbating market concerns about a chain reaction of institutional liquidations. However, business contraction does not equate to liquidation and forced liquidation. It's more about managers proactively controlling risk and adjusting their business model, rather than insolvency leading to bankruptcy. A timeline easily overlooked by the market is that hedge funds began reducing their positions and deleveraging as early as October, and the November 5th crash was more likely a concentrated realization of this process. Goldman Sachs Prime Brokerage data shows that in October, global fundamental equity long-short funds lost an average of about 3.5%, while systematic long-short strategy funds lost about 3.6%. This is the first time since Goldman Sachs began tracking this data in 2016 that both types of strategies have experienced losses exceeding 3% in the same month. Even more subtle actions occurred in mid-October. In just two weeks, Goldman Sachs' hedge fund clients net sold $20 billion worth of tech stocks; in just five trading days from October 8th to 14th, they wiped out all the net long positions in AI stocks accumulated since the beginning of 2025. By the end of October, the net leverage ratio of hedge funds had fallen to 73.4%, a monthly decrease of 4.2 percentage points, marking the largest monthly decline since March of this year. Morgan Stanley's data also reveals this change. Stock-picking hedge funds experienced their largest active reduction in positions in over a decade in October, with market exposure decreasing by approximately 9% since June. By the end of October, more than 40% of related funds had broken even or suffered losses year-to-date. However, hedge fund performance also showed significant divergence, with not the entire industry suffering losses. Coatue Management recorded a positive return of 0.2% in October, Citadel rose 1.7%, and Quantedge saw a monthly increase of 7.2%. While some stumbled in crowded trades, others profited from market volatility. The money didn't disappear; it just moved. Behind the trillions of dollars in market capitalization evaporated in the US stock market is a massive migration of funds. The money doesn't vanish into thin air; it simply flows out of highly volatile, highly leveraged tech stocks and into safer, more liquid assets. The largest destination is US Treasury bonds. On Thursday, the day of the US stock market crash, the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds fell to 4.84%, a new low since September. The inverse relationship between prices and yields indicates a significant influx of funds into the bond market. The second stop is the US dollar. Alex Kuptsikevich, Chief Market Strategist at FxPro, points out that the tech stock panic has dragged down risk appetite, and the dollar has regained support from substantial safe-haven buying. Chris Turner, Global Head of Markets at ING, similarly believes that investors are currently more willing to hold cash in dollar assets, and the market is closer to shifting towards dollar cash than withdrawing from the dollar. Just as the dollar is gaining popularity, the Korean won and New Taiwan dollar, which were unfairly punished by risk sentiment, are also regaining attention. Yesterday, Claudio Piron, Head of Asia FX and Interest Rate Strategy at Bank of America Global Research, pointed out that the New Taiwan dollar and Korean won also presented buying opportunities after the sell-off in AI stocks. The substantial current account surpluses of Taiwan and South Korea will provide "strong support" for investors to establish long positions. Another key judgment by Bank of America is that AI industry chain companies already have substantial capital expenditures and export orders, which will not be cancelled due to the decline in US stocks. Continued export revenue settlement over the next 6 to 12 months will provide new underlying support for the New Taiwan Dollar and the Korean Won. The selling spree has temporarily subsided, but position clearing may not be the end. Rapid rebounds after a sharp drop are not uncommon; the real challenge lies in distinguishing whether it marks the end of the decline or a temporary recovery. History doesn't repeat itself in detail, but it often rhymes. August 2007: Quantitative Funds Deleveraging From August 6th to 9th, 2007, numerous equity long-short quantitative funds suffered concentrated losses, resulting in a bloodbath in the market. Research by MIT scholars Amir Khandani and Andrew Lo found that the concentrated liquidation of crowded trades and the brief withdrawal of market-making capital jointly led to the abnormal liquidity at the time. The most severe phase of the sharp decline was concentrated in only four days; some strategies began to rebound after August 10th, but the entire deleveraging process continued from July to the end of the year. The sharp decline was just the prelude; the real position clearing and risk appetite recovery may take several months. March 2020: The pandemic triggered a comprehensive sell-off of risky assets. From February 19th to March 23rd, 2020, the S&P 500 fell by approximately 34%, and the correction lasted for more than a month, interspersed with several sharp single-day rebounds, until it finally recovered its losses in August of that year. In the short term, the performance of US stocks in the past two days is closer to the first scenario: the most intense concentrated selling may have passed, but the rebalancing of market positions and the recovery of risk appetite are far from over. This is precisely where the market divergence lies. Renowned investor Jason Calacanis stated that the market bottom may have appeared, but tech stock valuations could still fall by another 10%, which would be an ideal buying opportunity. Optimistic Bitmine Chairman Tom Lee believes that Thursday's US stock market crash was like an aftershock of a "blue tsunami" triggered by the midterm election results, a superposition of "last year's tariff shock + the DeepSeek moment + this June's Situational Awareness forced liquidation." Such concentrated selling often bottoms out within a few days, creating buying opportunities. US stock analyst Mark Minervini offered a more cautious assessment. He believes that while the decline in US stocks may not reach the level of the 1987 stock market crash, it could lay the foundation for some form of stock market collapse, which could last one to two weeks. If the decline intensifies, the worst-case scenario for the SPY is a 10%-15% drop from its peak. The Nasdaq could fall 20-25%, resulting in a cyclical bear market similar to 1998. Currently, the gains in US stocks last night are far from offsetting the previous day's losses. An asset that falls 20% needs to rise 25% to return to its original level. The Nasdaq, which fell 5.52% on Thursday, will still be significantly lower than its previous level even if it rises 1.1% the following day. After two days of sharp fluctuations, US stocks have reached a crossroads. The narrative that has driven the surge in AI tech stocks over the past few months is now facing a severe test of reality. While the short-term deleveraging may be coming to an end, the medium-term struggle surrounding issues such as the implementation of industry policies and the return on AI investment is only just entering its most complex phase.
